Introduction and meaning
Force. Historical concordance: IPC 349. For conduct governed by the BNS, cite BNS section 128; the IPC reference is historical concordance.
In student language: BNS s. 128 is the rule on “Force”. The section provides that a person is said to use force to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion as brings that substance into contact with any part of that other’s body, or with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other’s sense of feeling:. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 128 exists so that “Force” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
128. A person is said to use force to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion as brings that substance into contact with any part of that other’s body, or with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other’s sense of feeling:

(a) by his own bodily power;

(b) by disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion or change or cessation of motion takes place without any further act on his part, or on the part of any other person;

(c) by inducing any animal to move, to change its motion, or to cease to move

Essential ingredients
1. A person is said to use force to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion as brings that substance into contact with any part of that other’s body, or with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other’s sense of feeling:
2. (a) by his own bodily power;
3. (b) by disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion or change or cessation of motion takes place without any further act on his part, or on the part of any other person;
4. (c) by inducing any animal to move, to change its motion, or to cease to move

Exceptions, limitations and provisos
Provided that the person causing the motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion, causes that motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion in one of the following three ways, namely:–

hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 128 (Force), Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) A person is said to use force to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion as brings that substance into contact with any part of that other’s body, or with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other’s sense of feeling:
   (2) (a) by his own bodily power;
   (3) (b) by disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion or change or cessation of motion takes place without any further act on his part, or on the part of any other person;
   (4) (c) by inducing any animal to move, to change its motion, or to cease to move
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 128 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 128 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

learningObjectives: Master the physical definition of force under BNS s. 128.
Analyze the three mechanical forms: causing motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion.
Understand the three statutory instrumentalities: bodily power, disposing substances, or inducing animals.
Differentiate pure force from criminal force.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 128 defines force: a person is said to use force to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other, or causes any substance to come into contact with any part of that other's body, by his own bodily power, by disposing any substance, or by inducing any animal to move or change its motion.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Provides the foundational physics-based definition of human force in criminal law, establishing that any intentional alteration of another's kinetic state constitutes force.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 128 (corresponding to IPC s. 349).
Three effects: (1) Causing motion; (2) Change of motion; (3) Cessation of motion.
Three instrumentalities: (a) By own bodily power; (b) By disposing any substance; (c) By inducing any animal.
Purely definitional: Section 128 defines force; Section 129 adds mens rea to make it 'criminal force'.
essentialIngredients: The accused caused motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to another person; OR caused a substance to touch the other person's body or clothing.
The effect was produced by the accused's own bodily power; OR
By disposing of a substance such that the contact happens without further act; OR
By inducing an animal to move, change motion, or cease motion.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 128 is purely definitional. It establishes the mechanical meaning of 'force' as used in criminal jurisprudence. Force under Section 128 requires three alternative kinetic effects upon the victim: causing motion (pushing someone standing still), changing motion (deflecting someone walking), or stopping motion (seizing someone running). Furthermore, it covers bringing any substance into contact with the victim's body or clothing (throwing water, spitting, or throwing a stone). The means can be direct muscular power, mechanical/chemical disposition of substances, or setting an animal in motion (e.g., ordering a dog to attack). Force on its own is neutral; it becomes criminal only when accompanied by the unlawful intent or lack of consent defined in Section 129.
examples: Teaching example (Causing motion by bodily power): A person pushes a stationary bystander from behind, causing the bystander to stumble forward. This is using force by bodily power under s. 128.
Teaching example (Inducing animal): An accused commands his horse to gallop directly into a pedestrian, forcing the pedestrian to jump out of the way. This is causing motion by inducing an animal.
distinctions: Force (s. 128) vs Criminal Force (s. 129): Force is the physical act of altering motion or causing contact; Criminal force is force used without consent to commit an offence or cause injury, fear, or annoyance.
Force vs Assault (s. 130): Force involves actual physical contact or kinetic alteration; Assault is the preparatory gesture creating apprehension of imminent force.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether unfastening the mooring rope of a boat in which a passenger is sleeping, causing the boat to drift downriver, constitutes using force to the passenger.
Rule: Causing motion to a person by disposing of a substance or object constitutes force under BNS s. 128.
Application: Unfastening the rope caused the boat and the passenger to move downriver without further act.
Conclusion: The act constitutes using force under BNS s. 128.

keyTakeaways: Defines the mechanical concept of force in criminal law.
Covers causing, changing, or stopping motion, or causing contact.
Achieved by bodily power, disposing substances, or inducing animals.
Neutral by itself; requires Section 129 mens rea to become criminal.
